title: "Sivaya Nama! Om Nama Sivaya!"
translation_notes: The source JSON contains extraction units rather than reliable authorial paragraph boundaries. Continuous sentences and the long spoken journey through Thirukkuvalai are reconstructed from syntax and rhetorical movement; the joins are recorded in the source-note sidecar.
The repeated Tamil chapter title is represented in metadata rather than repeated as body prose. The invocation itself is transliterated rather than silently standardised into a Sanskrit form.

The extracted form 'நாள் கூட' in the Pattani-deity passage is rendered by its clear first-person contextual function ('I too, in those days...') and remains explicitly documented rather than silently normalised.

T2 established that 'அரிநமோத்து சிந்தம்' functions as an old education-initiation formula. The Tamilised source form is retained as 'Arinamothu Sindham' with only that minimal contextual gloss; no speculative word-for-word doctrinal translation is imposed.

T2 established that Postmaster Iyer's dated Brahmin-Tamil 'நோக்கு' functions as 'உனக்கு' ('for/to you') in 'தபால் வந்திருக்கு நோக்கு!'; the T1 mistranslation 'look!' has been corrected without inventing an English regional accent.
Concrete political images—the unhealed wound and punugu, surgery, and the kicked ball—are retained rather than replaced with abstract political summary.

Humour is preserved without explanatory after-commentary, including the thief who steals the pot of hair, the curd-and-village-pond joke, the Angalamman puja prompted by Appa's desire for chicken curry, and curse-soil blown back into devotees' own eyes.

T3 made only five English-language refinements after source recheck: the joy/sorrow memory phrase, the Muneeswaran punchline, the two-Avvaiyars body image, the family's happiness, and the rain-of-kisses image.
paragraphs: My parents left out none of the rites that orthodox parents were expected to perform for their children. My ear-piercing ceremony was conducted with great splendour. In the same way, I was sent off to school with much ceremony under the name of 'Vidyarambam,' the initiation into learning.

In the name of vows and prayers, the hair of my head was offered to many temples. Hair, of course, had to grow again; it seemed my very body had become a vow owed to one temple or another. They would shave my head and smear sandal paste over it. Even now, when I think of it, I laugh.

My parents had vowed to offer my hair at the Kaniyagurichi Mariamman temple. But when the appointed auspicious day came, there was no way for them to travel to that village. Do you know what they did? Without going to Kaniyagurichi, they shaved my head right there in our village, put the hair safely in a pot, kept it in the garden, and sent only the other offerings due to the Kaniyagurichi temple.

Appa and Amma kept saying that whenever someone happened to go there—or whenever someone from our own household went—they could take the pot along and offer my hair then. They guarded that pot anxiously, as though they were safeguarding something immensely valuable.

The thief who entered our house for the second time found everyone awake and could get hold of nothing. So, thinking that pot was a temple money-box, he picked it up and ran away with it. Only after he opened it would he have learned the truth!

Besides sending me to school, my father also arranged for me to learn music. But I developed no interest in musical training. Where the 'big men' were gathered, I could not go before them wearing a shirt. I had to remove even my upper cloth and tie it around my waist. Wearing sandals too was forbidden.

Such harsh bondage—subjecting a whole community to cruelty in the name of divinity, caste, religion, shastras and custom—roused my tender young mind to fierce opposition. That was why I came to hate the music lessons.

The social evils surrounding me became the cause of my awakening. Only one who has walked over stones and thorns can describe the pleasure of it, can he not? How can a man who has never stepped down from a golden, jewel-studded bed understand rough and rugged roads?

Ideas of reform that arise from upper castes, exalted lineages and elite households have, for the most part, done little more than smear punugu perfume upon an unhealed wound. Revolutionary voices that arise from backward communities possess the power to heal that unhealed wound by surgery. Like a ball that springs away with greater speed when kicked. A man who comes from an oppressed people sets out to wipe away degradation. He sets out in fury.

Understanding the direction of my mind, my father made me apply myself seriously to school. A private tutor was arranged for me too. As his pay, he was given a seer of fresh milk morning and evening, with vegetables from time to time. He was also the 'headmaster' of our village school.

While studying, I began acting in the village as well—in daytime plays! A school holiday was enough: I would turn our cowshed into a theatre. I was ten years old. A drama in the cowshed even then! In those performances I had an unquenchable desire to play Arjuna and Krishna. Appa was always telling stories about them; captivated by those characters, I would scoop up blue powder, smear it all over my body and act. Villagers would gather to watch our plays too.

Festivals were held frequently at the Thirukkuvalai temple. The very next day after a festival ended there, a festival in imitation of it would begin on the verandah of our house. I would make a 'sami' out of clay. We had a bronze toy of a Rishabha vahana, the bull mount. We would place the clay deity upon it, make the sounds of drums and instruments with our mouths, and conduct the deity's procession.

As I write this, the memory of that old bronze Rishabha-vahana toy has come back to me. Do you know how many fresh memories of my youth would flicker before me if I could search somewhere, find it again and look at it?

That slightly broken toy cannot possibly have vanished altogether. If I could find that toy, which has so many happy stories to tell, and place it before me on my desk, there would be no measure to that happiness.
Many years later I had an opportunity to visit the village where I was born. All along the way I kept telling my comrades memories of the old days, and within me I felt joy and pride.

What exhilaration there is in memories of youth! When an aged husband shows affection to his wife whose face has withered, whose skin has wrinkled and whose beauty has faded, does not the fullness of that love shine because, in his mind's eye, he remembers the full-moon face of her youth, her cheeks like the fleshy sides of a mango, and her gleaming form?

When the dry leaves of memory rise and fall, again and again, in the whirl of thought, only those who have experienced it can understand the peculiar exhilaration that comes over a human being—and, hidden within that exhilaration, the sorrow, steeped in feeling and mingled with joy. Even a master artist could not fully express such a feeling.
Dazed by just such a feeling, I am travelling along the road to Thirukkuvalai. In a car, with my comrades!

'Here—this village is Kachanam! When I studied at Tiruvarur, this was where I would get down from the bus. From here I would walk four or five miles to the village—not every day! On holidays! If I bought kara-boondi for an anna or two at the Kachanam coffee hotel and ate it as I walked, I would hardly notice the hardship of walking the road alone.'

'Sometimes I would have to walk alone at night. Fear would burst up inside my chest—thik-thik! For those journeys my father and an elder who was his friend, Saravana Swamiyar, taught me a mantra: “Sivaya Nama! Om Nama Sivaya!” I would walk muttering it under my breath. Ghosts and demons, they said, would not come near if they heard that mantra! That belief had struck deep roots in my young heart. Only now has that very root been yanked out and thrown away!'

'Here—this is Karugudi! Our village is only a mile from here. We had to come to this village to buy curd for our house. Carrying a lead vessel, two or three of us would set out as early as seven in the morning and come here. We would reach home with the curd at nine or ten. If we became thirsty on the way, we would drink a little of it. After all, villages have plenty of ponds precisely to make good whatever was missing!'

'Here—this wooded place. Do you know how frightened we once were of it? Inside it stands the shrine of an evil deity called Pattani. At night, they said, that deity would pass through the fields with his forces in a torchlight procession. Many people would insist they had seen the sight with their own eyes. The torchlike lights they saw were real enough. But how could they then have known that what they called Pattani's torch procession was a row of flames produced by a kind of sulphurous gas emerging from cracks in the fields? Even now many people are unwilling to accept that explanation! I too, in those days, believed it and trembled. I crossed these parts only with the help of the Namashivaya mantra.'

'While going that way, if even an owl cried out, that was enough—my heart would surely burst! And when people die from terror, their hearts bursting and blood coming from their mouths, do not devotees describe them as people who were struck dead by ghosts?'

'There—do you see that great figure sitting there, ruined, faded, mutilated? That is Muneeswaran. Whenever some calamity struck the village—when smallpox or cholera spread—that Muneeswaran would possess a man named Veerappa Velar, make him dance in frenzy, and through him offer comfort to the village. Now that Velar too is gone! Illness and disease still come to the village—but Muneeswaran no longer comes to grant protection. When he himself is in such straits, how can he come to help others?'
'Here it is, at the end of our street! This is the Angalamman temple! Whenever my Appa developed a desire to eat chicken curry, arrangements for a puja at the Angalamman temple would begin at once!'

'Among all the temples at which my head was repeatedly shaved, this one holds a place of distinction. We would come here often to tell all our family's grievances. It was a good place for the villagers to air grievances too. Many devotees would come to the temple entrance with the “good” thought that families they disliked should be destroyed and fling handfuls of earth as a curse. Sometimes the earth they threw would be caught by the wind and land in their own eyes!'

'Next to this temple—look, there it lies, collapsed almost to ground level! This is the temple of knowledge that made me what I am: the school where I studied. Ah! What torrents of feeling overflow their banks when I look at it! Is this not the place where I learned by writing and rewriting the old initiation formula “Arinamothu Sindham” in the sand until my fingertips wore down?'
'That tender age, with no anxiety or torment over what the future might hold, absorbed without care in the games of the present—can a human being ever encounter that age a second time?'

'The distress of being unable to find solutions to problems piled up like mountains, of turning whichever way only to see work waiting and not knowing how to finish it, of lamenting and suffering—that distress never once set foot near the happy years of youth! Is this school not entitled to the glory of having taken us, little sparrows who lived amid peals of laughter, and made us people strong enough to fly in the sky of life?'
'Beyond the school—here, all these houses you see in a row are the homes of my relatives! Ah! How many histories of the past rise before my mind's eye!'

'How many elders, how many masters of music, how many people with loving hearts once walked these streets! Where are they all now? How many families have disappeared like banyan trees uprooted by a storm!'

'Was it not along that pond bank that Vaidyalinga Mama would stand with his arms folded, gazing at the sky, eager to see whether Garuda would fly past and give him some good omen? Now he himself has flown away! Was it not here that Vaithi Thatha would bustle about with a spade in his hand, clearing the grass? And there, beneath that tree on the pond bank, was it not my beloved father who gave me life, hunting fish with his hook?'

'If just the bunch of keys hanging at the waist of Meikkaaval Kuppusami Thatha—the short man with the quick little gait—had gone missing, all the gods of the great temple would have had to starve! Every key to the temple was with him!'
'Hunched and shrunken like cats until the day they died, Thillaiamma and Vairiyatha were the two Avvaiyars of Thirukkuvalai!'

'None of them is here now. There—the verandahs of the agraharam, where people passed the time playing cards in the pleasure of the breeze... Across the pond, in one house, was the post office. As soon as the mail arrived, the Postmaster Iyer, standing on that bank of the pond, would call loudly to the houses on this bank: “Mail has come for you! Send the boy over! I'll send it!” We would run across and collect it. That scene has still not left the screen of my heart!'

'There—the house in which I crawled and played... How many stories of happiness and sorrow it tells me! I cannot go on looking at that house for long. Why? Alas—how many people have vanished within thirty years! The Karugudi vaidyar would come like a hospital itself moving toward us, as though carrying the entire dispensary in his lap, like the great Tiruvarur temple chariot. Where is he now?'
'Ratna Padayachi may have looked frail, but he had an unfailing firmness in his heart and affection for us; whenever we suffered, he gave comfort to our family. I cannot see him now either!'

The moment I entered the village, relatives and friends surrounded me and almost suffocated me with affection. 'Let what has happened remain what has happened; may what happens from now on be good,' they said. They renewed our bonds, smelled the crown of my head in affection, and lavished hospitality upon me.

At such moments I stood with tears in my eyes, thinking of my mother and father. Do you know how my mother and sisters brimmed with happiness when they heard how the people of my native village had embraced me, rejoiced over me, blessed me and sent me on my way?

Raining kisses upon me, mothers and elders had blessed me: 'Long live, son of Muthuvel!' It was leaving those people—and leaving the village where I had crawled and played—that, at the age of twelve, I set out for Tiruvarur to study.
I was taken there to be admitted to the Second Form at Tiruvarur High School. But the headmaster of the high school declared that I could not be admitted even to the Fifth Standard!
